purpose: Engineering failures and measured limitations are part of the reproducibility record, not noise to be deleted.

entries.failure: launcher process guard used a full-command-line match (pgrep -f), which matched the bash wrapper whose command text CONTAINED the script — false-positive 'run already active'
entries.effect: the watchdog would have refused every legitimate restart; with the host recycling every ~3 h, no corridor run would ever have advanced again
entries.detection: manual audit during a watchdog tick (launcher reported a run active while ps showed no python3 solver)
entries.correction: guard now matches only real python3 processes (ps comm=='python3' AND args ~ run_corridor.py)

entries.failure: corridor_analysis.py labelled a partial run FINAL because a stale meta.json from a short smoke test satisfied the completeness check
entries.effect: a partial probe series could have been reported as a final result
entries.detection: self-review of the first analysis output
entries.correction: completeness now requires the probe series to actually reach the run's target window
entries.affected_scientific_results: none — caught before any partial output was used in a claim

entries.failure: probe scheduler deadline (_next) was restored as time+interval instead of its saved value
entries.effect: a restart could silently skip one probe sample and shift the probe grid; probe continuity LOOKED fine while the schedule drifted
entries.detection: state audit prompted by external review before the wet-phase equivalence test
entries.correction: _next is now saved in and restored from the checkpoint; the wet-phase A/B test compares every probe record bitwise
entries.affected_scientific_results: none for completed analyses (all published probe series came from runs without a mid-interval restart of this kind)

entries.measured_limitation: the solver executes on ONE core (~100% CPU measured via /proc jiffies: 999/10 s), not four — elementwise NumPy kernels do not use BLAS threading
entries.consequence: sequential scheduling buys restart robustness and memory headroom, not compute acceleration; wall-time projections must assume single-core throughput
entries.decision: solver is NOT being rewritten or parallelized mid-experiment; the limitation is recorded instead

entries.measured_limitation: restart start-up cost dominated short process lifetimes: rebuilding nest terrain, roughness, culverts, probe geometry and the parent-derived stage BC took ~50 s, while the recycling host was giving processes only 2-5 minutes of life
entries.measurement: rate analysis of checkpoint log lines showed the SOLVER is not the bottleneck (~2 wall-min per model-hour in the dry phase); the run was losing most of each lifetime to deterministic setup
entries.correction: setup is now cached to a 1 MB npz and reloaded in 0.2 s (250x faster start-up). The cache is a pure function of frozen inputs, and tests/solver_equivalence/test_setup_cache.py proves the reconstruction is array-identical to a fresh build (z, roughness, mask, rain index map, culverts, probe groups, transform, CRS, stage BC).
entries.affected_scientific_results: none — verified identical before any cached run output was used

entries.failure: CHECKPOINT LIVELOCK — the wall-clock checkpoint interval (420 s) was longer than the host's shortest process lifetime (as little as 1-2 min), so every process died before its first checkpoint and the run resumed from the same model hour indefinitely
entries.observation: buckeye_c sat at model hour 6.50 with 390 probe samples for 37 minutes across three relaunches, each reporting a successful RESUME. Every individual component was working; the system as a whole made zero progress.
entries.why_it_hid: resume was verified as CORRECT (bit-identical) and start-up was verified as FAST (0.2 s). Both were true. The failure was in the interaction between checkpoint cadence and host lifetime, which neither component test could expose.
entries.correction: CKPT_WALL_S 420 s -> 60 s. Measured cost: 0.49 s per checkpoint (6.4 MB), i.e. 0.8% overhead. Progress is now monotonic.
entries.generalizable_lesson: a checkpoint interval must be shorter than the host's SHORTEST observed lifetime, not merely shorter than its average. Averages hide livelock.
entries.affected_scientific_results: none — no result was produced during the stalled period; the cost was wall-clock time only

entries.failure: MISDIAGNOSIS — concurrent corridor runs were abandoned for sequential execution on the belief that three solves on four cores 'were not converging before the next recycle'
entries.actual_cause: the runs were not converging because of the EF-4 checkpoint livelock (checkpoint interval longer than host lifetime), which applied equally to sequential execution. Core contention was not the cause.
entries.effect: three of four cores sat idle while a single-threaded solver ran; total throughput was roughly one third of what the host could deliver
entries.detection: a direct capacity check (nproc, load average, per-process CPU) prompted by the question of whether the work could be parallelised
entries.correction: parallel execution restored, capped at nproc-1 to leave a core for the OS and analysis tooling; priority order retained so the highest-value run starts first after a recycle
entries.affected_scientific_results: none — scheduling changes cannot alter a deterministic solve; the cost was wall-clock time only
entries.execution_environment_note: compute runs on a remote 4-core Intel Xeon @2.10GHz VM with 15 GB RAM and NO GPU (no NVIDIA device nodes, no CUDA). Local operator hardware is not involved in the computation. Any GPU or many-core acceleration is therefore a change of execution environment, not a code change, and is deliberately deferred until after this experiment.

entries.measured_limitation: buckeye_c solves 6-8x slower than the other corridors (1.83 model-hours per wall-hour vs 10.8 franklinton / 15.1 pataskala) despite fewer cells than pataskala and shallower water than franklinton
entries.diagnosis: its global CFL timestep is VELOCITY-limited at 21.35 m/s while the others are wave-limited at 3-4 m/s. The 21.35 m/s occurs on exactly 5 cells of the SOUTHERN DOMAIN EDGE, where the OPEN boundary places a ghost dry cell at the live cell's own bed: deep channel water therefore sees a free drop of its full depth over one cell width and exits at high speed. dt = cfl*dx/(v+sqrt(g*h)) is global, so five boundary cells throttle 0.68M cells.
ruled_out: thin-film velocity spike — the fastest face carries 882 mm of water and the value is identical at min_depth 1e-3, 1e-4 and 1e-5
stage-BC jet — max velocity anywhere on the BC ring is 1.39 m/s, and zero cells above 5 m/s lie within two cells of the ring
interior instability — interior maximum is 3.47 m/s with NO cells above 5 m/s anywhere in the domain
entries.physics_impact: none identified in the interior. The affected cells are the outflow boundary itself; the corridor probes are far inside. The free-outfall OPEN boundary is the pre-registered configuration and behaves as designed.
entries.decision: NOT changed. Altering the boundary treatment or the CFL velocity mid-experiment would change the frozen configuration and invalidate the comparison. The cost is wall-clock time only, and it is recorded rather than optimised away.
entries.for_future_work: a domain-edge outflow treatment (e.g. normal-depth or critical-depth outflow instead of free drop to bed), or excluding boundary faces from the global CFL reduction, would remove this throttle. Both are engine changes and belong to the aqua-sim backlog, not to this study.

generalisation.finding: NOT specific to buckeye. As water deepened, franklinton and pataskala became velocity-limited by the SAME open-boundary free-outfall mechanism.
generalisation.consequence: all three corridor runs converge on ~1 model-hour per wall-hour once their channels fill, because a few dozen outflow cells set the global timestep for the whole domain. This is a property of the OPEN boundary at a deep-water exit, not of any one site.

resolution.finding: the earlier 'franklinton INTERIOR 26.28 m/s' reading was WRONG, and wrong because of a flaw in the diagnostic, not in the model. See EF-6. Recomputed correctly, ML-3 explains franklinton and buckeye COMPLETELY: excluding a single cell ring from every edge drops franklinton's domain maximum from 26.48 to 4.96 m/s and leaves ZERO faces above 5 m/s anywhere in 875,362 interior faces. Buckeye has no face above 5 m/s at all, and falls from 3.12 to 0.68 m/s at two rings.
resolution.pataskala_is_the_exception_and_it_is_phy: pataskala is the only nest with fast flow deep in the interior: 35 faces above 5 m/s more than 5 cell rings from any edge. Those are NOT a numerical thin film. Median conveyance depth is 2.43 m and median Froude 1.39, with 21 of 35 carrying more than 1 m of water at channel roughness (n = 0.024-0.035) — this is the South Fork Licking mainstem in flood, which is what the nest was built to resolve. The remaining 6 (conveyance depth ~0.2 m, Froude ~4, road roughness n = 0.013) are shallow sheet flow spilling road embankments; they carry negligible volume and are the expected local-inertial behaviour at an embankment crest.
resolution.consequence_for_interpretation: the blocker on franklinton is REMOVED. Its results may be interpreted. No corridor probe in any nest sits in fast water attributable to the boundary: franklinton's science probes are 82-96 cells inside the domain at 0.35-0.42 m/s, and buckeye's are 28-296 cells inside and still dry at hour 7.73.
resolution.caveats_created: two probe groups touch the domain edge and must carry a declared caveat rather than being read as interior results: franklinton olentangy_gauge_03227107 (and its __channel pair) at 0 cells from the edge, and pataskala us40_etna__channel at 1 cell. Both are currently slow (0.65 and 0.58 m/s) so neither is contaminated at present, but their values are boundary-influenced by construction and are reported as such.
resolution.evidence: analysis/boundary_velocity_audit.py + analysis/boundary_velocity_audit.json (read-only recomputation from the checkpointed states; nothing written back into any run)

entries.measured_limitation: the execution container is torn down between interactive turns, so the solver only advances WHILE A TURN IS ACTIVE. Background processes do not accumulate compute in the gaps.
entries.measurement: summed process wall time from the checkpoint logs against elapsed clock time since the corridor runs began: buckeye 62.2 min solved / 492 min elapsed = 12.6% duty cycle; franklinton 9.5%; pataskala 9.8%. Cross-check on a single interval: 72 min of clock time between watchdog ticks yielded 0.14 model-hours for buckeye, which at its measured 1.83 model-h per wall-hour is 4.6 min of compute — approximately the length of the turn itself.
entries.why_it_hid: every individual mechanism worked. Checkpoint/resume was proven bit-identical, start-up was cached to 0.2 s, the livelock was fixed, and parallelism was restored. Each watchdog tick honestly reported progress. The runs were simply frozen between ticks, and no per-component test could show that.
entries.consequence: polling on an hourly watchdog cannot finish these runs. Remaining compute at measured rates: franklinton ~57 min, pataskala ~37 min, buckeye ~6.8 hours (buckeye inflated ~5x by the ML-3 boundary CFL throttle). At a few minutes of compute per tick, buckeye alone would need on the order of 100 ticks.
entries.affected_scientific_results: none — no result is altered, only deferred. The Case B determination rests on surveyed geometry and observed gauge timing, neither of which depends on these runs.
entries.implication_for_future_work: sustained simulation needs an execution environment that persists between interactions. This is the concrete justification for moving compute off this platform before any regional-scale benchmark.

entries.title: Self-caught measurement error: 'interior' velocity diagnostic did not exclude the boundary CELL ROW
entries.what_i_reported: that franklinton's interior maximum face velocity was 26.28 m/s, unlike buckeye's 3.47 m/s, and that this was 'NOT explained by the boundary alone' and 'worth investigating separately before franklinton's results are interpreted'. That was committed to this repository at b4900d8 and was wrong.
entries.root_cause: the diagnostic separated 'interior' from 'edge' by excluding the solver's BOUNDARY FACES — the ghost faces outside the edge cells. But the faces BETWEEN adjacent cells within the edge row are interior faces by that classification, and they are exactly the faces carrying the lateral drawdown that feeds the free outfall. Excluding boundary faces therefore does not isolate the interior; whole cell ROWS must be excluded.
entries.how_it_was_caught: by asking where the fast faces actually are instead of only how fast they are. All five franklinton faces above 5 m/s sit at j=697 — the last row of a 698-row domain — at distance 0 from the edge.
entries.correction: recomputed as a function of how many cell rings are excluded from every edge. franklinton 26.48 -> 4.96 m/s after one ring, with zero faces above 5 m/s thereafter. Recorded under ML-3.resolution.
entries.impact_of_the_error: it would have suppressed or delayed interpretation of a franklinton result that is in fact sound. It did not affect any model output, forcing, geometry or parameter — the defect was in the diagnostic only, and the diagnostic is read-only.
entries.lesson: a scalar extremum is not a diagnosis. Report WHERE an extremum lives before concluding WHAT it is; a spatial profile would have shown in one line what a maximum concealed.
entries.kept_visible: the incorrect claim is not deleted from history — commit b4900d8 stands and this entry names it.

entries.title: Run crashed writing meta.json AFTER completing, because the setup-cache path leaves a variable unbound
entries.what_happened: corridor_pataskala_c_B reached its target t=20.0000 h and wrote state.npz, probes.json, peak.npz and snaps.npz — every scientific output — then died with UnboundLocalError on 'bcp' while serialising meta.json, and never printed COMPLETE.
entries.root_cause: 'bcp' (the boundary-stage file path) is assigned only inside the COLD-SETUP branch. The ML-2 setup-cache fix added a second path that skips that branch entirely, so any run that restored from cache — which is every long run, by design — reached the metadata writer with 'bcp' unbound. The two fixes were individually correct and jointly broken.
entries.why_it_mattered_more_than_it_looks: the run looked failed. Without checking the log against the state file it would have been natural to relaunch it as if hours of compute had been lost, or to mark the nest incomplete. The EF-2 discipline — completeness means the probe series reaches meta['hours'], not that a file exists — is what made the true state legible.
entries.fix: derive the label from the CLI argument a.bcfile, which is defined on both paths, instead of the branch-local bcp.
entries.recovery: relaunched after the fix. The run restored from checkpoint at model hour 20.00, executed zero steps, wrote meta.json, and printed COMPLETE. probes.json and peak.npz were rewritten BYTE-IDENTICALLY (md5 verified before and after) — an unplanned live confirmation of the checkpoint-equivalence property that test_checkpoint_equivalence.py asserts synthetically.
entries.lesson: a caching fast path is a second control-flow path, and every variable the slow path binds must be bound on it too. The failure surfaced at the last line of the program, which is the most expensive place to find it.

entries.title: gauge_timing.py used ndarray.ptp(), removed in NumPy 2.0
entries.what_happened: AttributeError: 'numpy.ndarray' object has no attribute 'ptp' when computing the normalised shape correlation.
entries.root_cause: the method form was removed in NumPy 2.0; this environment pins numpy 2.4.6. The line had never executed before because it is reached only when BOTH a model series and an observed series are present and overlap by more than an hour — i.e. only on a completed run with a gauge inside the nest.
entries.lesson: the code path that only runs at the very end of a successful experiment is the least-tested code in the project. Worth exercising deliberately on a smoke run rather than discovering at the finish line.
